paragraphs.heading: A blazing galactic core
paragraphs.text: A quasar is an active galactic nucleus, or AGN, that shines extremely brightly. Quasars are also called quasi-stellar objects, or QSOs for short. Astronomers usually treat them as one subclass within the wider family of AGN.

paragraphs.heading: What powers it
paragraphs.text: An AGN gets its power from gas falling onto a supermassive black hole, a process called accretion. That black hole has a mass anywhere from millions to tens of billions of times that of the Sun, and a disc of gas surrounds it. As gas in the disc sinks inward, it heats up and gives off energy as electromagnetic radiation. The total is enormous: the strongest quasars outshine a galaxy like the Milky Way thousands of times over.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name came from
paragraphs.text: Radio astronomy began in the 1950s, and it turned up a small number of odd objects among the galaxies. They poured out radio waves, yet photographs showed no clear source, or at most a faint dot that looked like a star. People called them quasi-stellar, meaning star-like, radio sources, and that mouthful was cut down to quasar. The first two, 3C 48 and 3C 273, were found in the late 1950s in radio surveys covering the whole sky.

paragraphs.heading: The 3C 273 breakthrough
paragraphs.text: The puzzle began to crack with 3C 273, which the Moon passed in front of. Radio measurements taken during one of those passes let Maarten Schmidt find its visible partner and record its spectrum with the 200-inch Hale Telescope. The spectrum had strange lines, and Schmidt showed they were most likely ordinary hydrogen lines, redshifted by 15.8%. If that redshift was cosmological, 3C 273 had to be very far away, which meant it was far brighter than any galaxy yet much more compact.

paragraphs.heading: Small but enormously powerful
paragraphs.text: 3C 273 is bright enough to show up on old photographs going back to the 1900s. Those records show its brightness changing over a year or so. That means much of its light comes from a region under one light-year across, which is tiny next to a galaxy. Some of these objects change brightness even faster, especially in X-rays, hinting that they may be no bigger than our Solar System and must pack huge power into that space.

paragraphs.heading: Where and when we find them
paragraphs.text: Sharp images, many from the Hubble Space Telescope, show that quasars sit at the centres of galaxies. Some of those host galaxies are interacting strongly with, or merging into, other galaxies. About a million quasars have reliable redshifts measured from their spectra. The nearest known one is about 600 million light-years away. Surveys also show quasars were more common long ago, with a peak roughly 10 billion years in the past.
